items.readable_text:
Content:
A common type of improper integral is one where the integrand (i.e., the function being integrated) is an exponential function.

Content:
For example, let's consider the following integral:

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-\infty}^{1} e^{x} \,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
This is an improper integral because the lower limit is unbounded. It can be interpreted as the shaded area under the curve [MATH: y=e^{x}] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2a1caaac52eba4edfa1349a021c2021d]

Content:
We proceed as we would with any other improper integral. We set the lower bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a], integrate, and take the limit as [MATH: a \to -\infty{:}]

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{1}e^{x}dx|= lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{1}e^{x}dx; = lim_(a → − ∞)[e^{x}]_{a}^{1}; = lim_(a → − ∞)(e^{1} − e^{a}); = lim_(a → − ∞)(e − e^{a})]

Content:
Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=e^x,] shown in the graph above:

Content:
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^x = 0]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^x = \infty]

Content:
Knowing this, we can solve our integral by evaluating the limit:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{1}e^{x}dx|= lim_(a → − ∞)(e − e^{a}); = e − 0; = e]

key_prerequisites.name: Integrating Exponential Functions Using Linear Substitution

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the following result:

[MATH: \int e^{px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1p e^{px+q} + C]

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.]

[MATH: ∫_{− 1}^{∞}e^{− 3x}dx|= lim_(a → ∞)∫_{− 1}^{a}e^{− 3x}dx; = lim_(a → ∞)[− (e^{− 3x})/(3)]_{− 1}^{a}; = − (1)/(3) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[e^{− 3x}]_{− 1}^{a}; = − (1)/(3) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)e^{− 3a} − e^{3})]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=e^{-3x}] shown in the graph below:

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^{-3x} = \infty]

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^{-3x} =0]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

[MATH: ∫_{− 1}^{∞}e^{− 3x}|= − (1)/(3) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)e^{− 3a} − e^{3}); = − (1)/(3) ⋅ (0 − e^{3}); = (e^{3})/(3).]

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the following result:

[MATH: \int b^{\,px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1{p\ln(b)} b^{\,px+q} + C]

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to-\infty.]

[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}3 ⋅ 2^{2x + 1}dx|= 3 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)∫_{a}^{0}2^{2x + 1}dx; = 3 ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)[(2^{2x + 1})/(2\ln (2))]_{a}^{0}; = (3 ⋅ 2^{1})/(2\ln (2)) ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)[2^{2x}]_{a}^{0}; = (3)/(\ln (2)) ⋅ lim_(a → − ∞)(2^{0} − 2^{2a}); = (3)/(\ln (2)) ⋅ (1 − lim_(a → − ∞)2^{2a})]

Now, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=2^{2x}] shown in the graph below:

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} 2^{2x} = 0]

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} 2^{2x} = \infty]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

[MATH: ∫_{− ∞}^{0}3 ⋅ 2^{2x + 1}dx|= (3)/(\ln (2)) ⋅ (1 − lim_(a → − ∞)2^{2a}); = (3)/(\ln (2)) ⋅ (1 − 0); = (3)/(\ln (2)).]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we substitute [MATH: u=x^4.] Differentiating, we get [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 4x^3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 14 \textrm{d}u =x^3\textrm{d}x.]

Since [MATH: u\to \infty] when [MATH: x\to \infty,] the table for the limits of integration using the rule [MATH: u=x^4] is as follows:

[MATH: x]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: \infty]

[MATH: u]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: \infty]

So, the integral in terms of the new variable [MATH: u] is [MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}x^{3} ⋅ 2^{− x^{4}}dx|= (1)/(4)∫_{1}^{∞}2^{− u}du.] Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.]

[MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}x^{3} ⋅ 2^{− x^{4}}dx|= (1)/(4)∫_{1}^{∞}2^{− u}du; = (1)/(4) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{1}^{a}2^{− u}du; = (1)/(4) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[− (2^{− u})/(\ln 2)]_{1}^{a}; = − (1)/(4\ln 2) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[2^{− u}]_{1}^{a}; = − (1)/(4\ln 2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)(1)/(2^{a}) − (1)/(2))]

Next, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2^x},] shown in the graph below:

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = \infty]

  • [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = 0]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

[MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}x^{3} ⋅ 2^{− x^{4}}dx|= − (1)/(4\ln 2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)(1)/(2^{a}) − (1)/(2)); = − (1)/(4\ln 2) ⋅ (0 − (1)/(2)); = (1)/(8\ln 2).]

Item 9 — Example: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_1^\infty x^3\cdot 2^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we substitute [MATH: u=x^4.] Differentiating, we get
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 4x^3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac 14 \textrm{d}u =x^3\textrm{d}x.]

Since [MATH: u\to \infty] when [MATH: x\to \infty,] the table for the limits of integration using the rule [MATH: u=x^4] is as follows:

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \infty] |
| [MATH: u] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \infty] |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable [MATH: u] is
[MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}x^{3} ⋅ 2^{− x^{4}}dx|= (1)/(4)∫_{1}^{∞}2^{− u}du.]
Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter [MATH: a,] integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as [MATH: a\to\infty.]

[MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}x^{3} ⋅ 2^{− x^{4}}dx|= (1)/(4)∫_{1}^{∞}2^{− u}du; = (1)/(4) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)∫_{1}^{a}2^{− u}du; = (1)/(4) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[− (2^{− u})/(\ln 2)]_{1}^{a}; = − (1)/(4\ln 2) ⋅ lim_(a → ∞)[2^{− u}]_{1}^{a}; = − (1)/(4\ln 2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)(1)/(2^{a}) − (1)/(2))]

Next, recall the end behavior of the function [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2^x},] shown in the graph below:

- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = \infty]
- [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = 0]

[IMG: /graphics/769170756b4db689d820f57e3f8d9791]

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

[MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}x^{3} ⋅ 2^{− x^{4}}dx|= − (1)/(4\ln 2) ⋅ (lim_(a → ∞)(1)/(2^{a}) − (1)/(2)); = − (1)/(4\ln 2) ⋅ (0 − (1)/(2)); = (1)/(8\ln 2).]
